etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from French thermomètre; equivalent to thermo- +‎ -meter.

definitions.definition: An apparatus used to measure temperature.

quote.citation: 1835, John Ross, James Clark Ross, Narrative of a Second Voyage in Search of a North-west Passage …, Volume 1‎[1], pages 284–5:
quote.text: Towards the following morning, the thermometer fell to 5°; and at daylight, there was not an atom of water to be seen in any direction.

quote.citation: 1843, John Holmes Agnew, Eclectic Museum of Foreign Literature, Science and Art:
quote.text: On the wall were hanging thermometers, barometers, and hydrometers, and every other sort of ometer, numberless, dusty, and mysterious;  […]

quote.citation: 1978, Jan Romein, The Watershed of Two Eras: Europe in 1900, page 303:
quote.text: Elsewhere, professionals could enthuse over new precision instruments capable, for instance, of measuring weights down to a tenth of a milligram, or over a host of self-registering thermometers and barometers, microscopes, typewriters, calculators and all sorts of technical and musical devices, including automatic concertinas, edeophones, auto-harps, bigophones and other long-forgotten objects.

quote.citation: 1992 March 2, Richard Preston, “The Mountains of Pi”, in The New Yorker:
quote.text: The brothers had thrust the thermometer between two circuit boards in order to look for hot spots inside m zero. The thermometer’s dial was marked “Beef Rare—Ham—Beef Med—Pork.” “You want to keep the machine below ‘Pork,’” Gregory remarked.
